chapter.name: The Other Side of Zero
chapter.blurb: Extending the number line to the left of zero: positive and negative numbers introduced through a lift moving between floors of a multi-storey building, integers defined as ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...; addition as Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor and subtraction as Target Floor - Starting Floor = Movement needed, both on a number line and with an unmarked number line; the token model, where a positive and a negative token cancel as a 'zero pair'; comparing integers with < and >; real-life integer contexts -- bank credit/debit, height above and depth below sea level, temperature; border-sum integer grid puzzles and the 'amazing grid' game; and the history of negative numbers in China and India, ending with Brahmagupta's 628 CE rules for adding and subtracting positive numbers, negative numbers and zero.

scope_in.item: Positive and negative numbers introduced via a lift's '+' and '-' buttons in a multi-storey building; zero (the ground floor) is neither positive nor negative
Numbering floors above and below a reference ground floor (Floor 0) using positive and negative numbers
Integers as the numbers ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ..., extending without end in both directions
Addition of integers as Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor, including combining several button presses
Additive inverse: a number plus its inverse equals zero
Comparing integers using floors and the symbols < and >
Subtraction of integers as Target Floor - Starting Floor = Movement needed, linked to "finding the missing number to be added"
Representing integers on a number line and adding/subtracting by counting steps forward or backward on it
Using an unmarked number line (UNL) to add and subtract larger integers
Converting subtraction of an integer into addition of its inverse, and vice versa
The token model: positive (green) and negative (red) tokens, and a "zero pair" of one of each having value zero
Adding integers with tokens by combining piles and cancelling zero pairs
Subtracting integers with tokens, adding extra zero pairs first when there are not enough tokens of the needed colour to remove
Bank credits (positive) and debits (negative), and finding an account balance as their total, including that a balance can temporarily be negative
Geographical heights above sea level (positive) and depths below sea level (negative), with sea level as 0 m
Temperature in degrees Celsius, measured above or below the freezing point of water (0 degC) as positive or negative integers
Border-integer-square puzzles, where the top row, bottom row, leftmost column and rightmost column of a grid each add to the same "border sum"
The "amazing grid" game, where circling one unstruck number per round (striking out its row and column each time) always gives the same total
Word problems, sequences and year-based (before/after a reference year) problems applying addition and subtraction of integers
The history of negative numbers in China (The Nine Chapters on Mathematical Art, using red and black rods) and India (Kautilya's Arthashastra, and the Bakhshali manuscript)
Brahmagupta's Rules for Addition and Subtraction of positive numbers, negative numbers and zero, from the Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta, 628 CE

concepts.name: Positive and Negative Numbers, and Comparing Integers
concepts.description: Numbers below zero are written with a '-' sign; together with positive numbers and zero they form the integers, which can be compared and ordered on a number line.
concepts.idea: Every whole number has a mirror-image negative partner on the other side of zero; the further left a number sits on the number line, the smaller it is.
concepts.rule: A number with a '+' sign (or no sign at all) is positive; a number with a '-' sign is negative; zero is neither. On the number line, smaller numbers are to the left, so between any two integers, the one further right is the greater.
concepts.example: Floor +5 is above Floor +3, so +5 > +3. Floor -4 is below Floor -3, so -4 < -3.

concepts.name: Addition and Subtraction of Integers as Movement
concepts.description: Addition of integers is found as Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor, and subtraction as Target Floor - Starting Floor = Movement needed; subtraction of any integer can be rewritten as addition of its additive inverse.
concepts.idea: Moving up and down floors in a lift matches adding and subtracting integers exactly: press '+' to add, '-' to subtract, and to undo a press you press its opposite (the additive inverse).
concepts.rule: Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor; equivalently, Target Floor - Starting Floor = Movement needed. A number and its additive inverse always add to zero. Subtracting a number gives the same result as adding its additive inverse.
concepts.example: From Floor +2, pressing -7 lands on Floor -5: (+2) + (-7) = -5. So (-5) - (+2) = -7, and (+2) - (+7) also equals (+2) + (-7) = -5.

concepts.name: The Token Model for Adding and Subtracting Integers
concepts.description: Positive (green) and negative (red) tokens can be combined and cancelled in pairs (zero pairs) to add and subtract integers, including adding extra zero pairs when there are not enough tokens of one colour to remove.
concepts.idea: A positive token and a negative token together are worth nothing, so any number of matching pairs can be added to or removed from a pile of tokens without changing its value.
concepts.rule: To add integers with tokens, combine the piles and cancel all zero pairs; what is left is the sum. To subtract, try to remove the tokens of the number being subtracted; if there are not enough, add zero pairs first until there are, then remove them.
concepts.example: (+5) + (-8): combine 5 green and 8 red tokens, cancel 5 zero pairs, 3 red tokens remain, so the answer is -3. (+5) - (+6): only 5 green tokens are available, so add one zero pair to get 6 green and 1 red, remove 6 green, leaving -1.

concepts.name: Integers in Real-Life Contexts
concepts.description: Positive and negative integers describe bank credits and debits, heights and depths measured from sea level, and temperatures above and below 0 degrees Celsius.
concepts.idea: Any situation with a natural zero point and two opposite directions (up/down, in/out, above/below) can be measured using positive and negative integers.
concepts.rule: Credits (money in) are positive, debits (money out) are negative, and the balance is their total; heights above sea level are positive and depths below are negative; temperatures above 0 degC are positive and below 0 degC are negative.
concepts.example: Starting balance 100 rupees, a credit of 60 rupees and a debit of 30 rupees give a new balance of 100 + 60 - 30 = 130 rupees. A depth of 200 m below sea level is written -200.

concepts.name: Integer Puzzles: Border-Sum Grids and Patterned Sums
concepts.description: In a border integer square, every row and column of the border adds to the same 'border sum'; in the 'amazing grid' game, circling one unstruck number per round always gives the same total, whichever numbers are chosen.
concepts.idea: A grid can be built so that many different selections of its numbers add up to the very same total, revealing a hidden pattern.
concepts.rule: To find a border sum, add all the numbers in one full row or column of the border; to complete a border-sum puzzle, fill unknown cells so every border row and column reaches the target sum.
concepts.example: In a grid with top row 4, -1, -3, the border sum is 4 + (-1) + (-3) = 0.

concepts.name: History of Negative Numbers and Brahmagupta's Rules
concepts.description: Negative numbers first appeared in ancient China (the Nine Chapters, using red and black rods) and India (Kautilya's Arthashastra, the Bakhshali manuscript), and Brahmagupta gave the first complete rules for adding and subtracting positive numbers, negative numbers and zero in 628 CE.
concepts.idea: Zero and negative numbers were used in accounting long before they were accepted as numbers in the rest of the world's mathematics.
concepts.rule: Brahmagupta's Rules for Addition: positive + positive = positive; negative + negative = negative (add the sizes, keep the minus sign); positive + negative = subtract the smaller size from the larger and take the sign of the larger; a number plus its inverse is zero; a number plus zero is unchanged. Rules for Subtraction: subtracting a negative number is the same as adding the corresponding positive number; a number minus itself is zero.
concepts.example: Brahmagupta's Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta (628 CE) gives (-5) + 3 = -2, since 5 - 3 = 2 and the larger size (5) was negative.
